claim: Drosophila larvae and adults possess a potent innate immune response.
source: Drosophila larvae and adults possess a potent innate immune response, but the response of Drosophila eggs is poor.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data or citations provided in this sentence.

claim: The response of Drosophila eggs is poor.
source: Drosophila larvae and adults possess a potent innate immune response, but the response of Drosophila eggs is poor.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract, and is further supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Eggs of the beetle Tribolium are protected by a serosa.
source: In contrast to Drosophila, eggs of the beetle Tribolium are protected by a serosa, an extraembryonic epithelium that is present in all insects except higher flies.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Tribolium anatomy.

claim: The serosa is an extraembryonic epithelium that is present in all insects except higher flies.
source: In contrast to Drosophila, eggs of the beetle Tribolium are protected by a serosa, an extraembryonic epithelium that is present in all insects except higher flies.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and is supported by citations elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: Bacteria propagate twice as fast in serosa-less eggs compared to wild-type eggs.
source: First, we show that bacteria propagate twice as fast in serosa-less eggs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1 showing bacterial growth rates.

claim: Infection induces genes involved in Toll and IMD-signaling in wild-type eggs but not in serosa-less eggs.
source: Infection induces genes involved in Toll and IMD-signaling, melanisation, production of reactive oxygen species and antimicrobial peptides in wild-type eggs but not in serosa-less eggs.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data comparing wild-type and Tc-zen1 RNAi eggs.

claim: Infection induces genes involved in melanisation in wild-type eggs but not in serosa-less eggs.
source: Infection induces genes involved in Toll and IMD-signaling, melanisation, production of reactive oxygen species and antimicrobial peptides in wild-type eggs but not in serosa-less eggs.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data comparing wild-type and Tc-zen1 RNAi eggs.

claim: Infection induces genes involved in production of reactive oxygen species in wild-type eggs but not in serosa-less eggs.
source: Infection induces genes involved in Toll and IMD-signaling, melanisation, production of reactive oxygen species and antimicrobial peptides in wild-type eggs but not in serosa-less eggs.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data comparing wild-type and Tc-zen1 RNAi eggs.

claim: Infection induces genes involved in antimicrobial peptide production in wild-type eggs but not in serosa-less eggs.
source: Infection induces genes involved in Toll and IMD-signaling, melanisation, production of reactive oxygen species and antimicrobial peptides in wild-type eggs but not in serosa-less eggs.
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data comparing wild-type and Tc-zen1 RNAi eggs.

claim: The serosal epithelium expresses immune genes constitutively and upon induction.
source: Finally, we demonstrate constitutive and induced immune gene expression in the serosal epithelium using in situ hybridization.
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: The serosa provides insect eggs with a full-range innate immune response.
source: We conclude that the serosa provides insect eggs with a full-range innate immune response.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combined experimental data from bacterial growth assays, RNAseq, and in situ hybridization.

claim: The humoral immune response is characterized by the massive secretion of antimicrobial peptides into the hemolymph and is mainly exerted by the fat body.
source: The humoral immune response is characterized by the massive secretion of antimicrobial peptides into the hemolymph and is mainly exerted by the fat body.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insect immunity, supported by the citations provided in the sentence (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007; Ganesan et al., 2011; Davis and Engstrom, 2012; Ferrandon, 2013; Ligoxygakis, 2013; Wang et al., 2014).

claim: Epithelia and hemocytes play the main role in local immune defenses that comprise melanisation, local AMP production, phagocytosis, and encapsulation.
source: Epithelia and hemocytes play the main role in local immune defenses that comprise melanisation, local AMP production, phagocytosis, and encapsulation (Lemaitre and Hoffmann, 2007; Ganesan et al., 2011; Davis and Engstrom, 2012; Ferrandon, 2013; Ligoxygakis, 2013; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The meso-diaminopimelic acid-type (DAP-type) peptidoglycans of Gram-negative bacteria activate the IMD pathway.
source: The meso-diaminopimelic acid-type (DAP-type) peptidoglycans of Gram-negative bacteria activate the IMD pathway, whereas the Lys-type peptidoglycans of Gram-positive bacteria activate the Toll pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insect immune signaling pathways.

claim: The Lys-type peptidoglycans of Gram-positive bacteria activate the Toll pathway.
source: The meso-diaminopimelic acid-type (DAP-type) peptidoglycans of Gram-negative bacteria activate the IMD pathway, whereas the Lys-type peptidoglycans of Gram-positive bacteria activate the Toll pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insect immune signaling pathways.

claim: Components of intracellular immune signaling pathways (Toll, IMD, and JAK/STAT) in Drosophila are 1:1 conserved in Tribolium.
source: Comparative genome analysis has revealed that components of intracellular immune signaling pathways (Toll, IMD, and JAK/STAT) in Drosophila are 1:1 conserved in Tribolium (Zou et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zou et al., 2007.

claim: The IMD and Toll pathway are largely functionally conserved between Drosophila and Tribolium.
source: The RNAi knockdown technology has shown that the IMD and Toll pathway are largely functionally conserved (Shrestha and Kim, 2010; Yokoi et al., 2012a, 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to RNAi studies.

claim: Serratia bacteria have been found inside eggs of corn earworms and corn borers.
source: Serratia bacteria, for instance, have been found inside eggs of corn earworms and corn borers (Bell, 1969; Lynch et al., 1976) and can infect eggs in the laboratory (Sikorowski et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bell, 1969 and Lynch et al., 1976.

claim: Serratia can infect eggs in the laboratory.
source: Serratia bacteria, for instance, have been found inside eggs of corn earworms and corn borers (Bell, 1969; Lynch et al., 1976) and can infect eggs in the laboratory (Sikorowski et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sikorowski et al., 2001.

claim: Serratia infection leads to reduced egg survival in the burying beetle Nicrophorus vespilloides.
source: We have also shown that Serratia infection leads to reduced egg survival in the burying beetle Nicrophorus vespilloides (Jacobs et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Female medflies cover their eggs with antimicrobial secretions.
source: Female medflies, for example, cover their eggs with antimicrobial secretions (Marchini et al., 1997) and in the absence of maternal care, eggs of earwigs die of fungal infection (Boos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Marchini et al., 1997.

claim: In the absence of maternal care, eggs of earwigs die of fungal infection.
source: Female medflies, for example, cover their eggs with antimicrobial secretions (Marchini et al., 1997) and in the absence of maternal care, eggs of earwigs die of fungal infection (Boos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Boos et al., 2014.

claim: The antimicrobial activity of eggs is of internal origin.
source: Two studies focusing on transgenerational immune priming, however, have shown that the antimicrobial activity of eggs is of internal origin (Sadd and Schmid-Hempel, 2007; Zanchi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sadd and Schmid-Hempel, 2007 and Zanchi et al., 2012.

claim: Drosophila eggs do not show induction of antimicrobial peptides until late stage 15.
source: It is not until late stage 15, (one of the latest stages in development when ectoderm and trachea have differentiated), that eggs show up to 25-fold upregulation of antimicrobial peptides (Tan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tan et al., 2014.

claim: Stage 11 Drosophila embryos cannot contain an infection of non-pathogenic bacteria, leading to reduced survival.
source: Except for Cecropin (Tingvall et al., 2001), stage 11 embryos do not show any induction of antimicrobial peptides and cannot contain an infection of non-pathogenic bacteria, leading to reduced survival (Tan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tingvall et al., 2001 and Tan et al., 2014.

claim: Tribolium eggs can upregulate several AMPs to levels comparable to the adult.
source: In strong contrast, we have shown that the eggs of Tribolium which were not even half way during development could upregulate several AMPs to levels comparable to the adult (Jacobs and van der Zee, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: AMP upregulation in Tribolium eggs depends on the serosa.
source: This upregulation depends on the serosa, an extraembryonic epithelium that envelopes yolk and embryo (Jacobs and van der Zee, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The serosa was lost in a small group of higher Diptera (the Schizophora) to which Drosophila belongs.
source: This membrane is present in all insects but was lost in a small group of higher Diptera (the Schizophora) to which Drosophila belongs (Schmidt-Ott, 2000; Rafiqi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schmidt-Ott, 2000 and Rafiqi et al., 2008.

claim: The NF-kappaB factor Dorsal is highly expressed in the presumptive serosa.
source: This has been suggested before, as the NF-kappaB factor Dorsal is highly expressed in the presumptive serosa (Chen et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2000.

claim: Tc-zen1 RNAi generates Tribolium eggs with an amnion at the dorsal side, but without a serosa.
source: In this beetle, we can prevent the development of the serosa by parental RNA interference with Tc-zerknüllt1 (Tc-zen1). This technique generates Tribolium eggs with an amnion at the dorsal side, but without a serosa (van der Zee et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to van der Zee et al., 2005.

claim: Normal larvae hatch from Tc-zen1 RNAi eggs at the relative humidity of the air of the laboratory.
source: At the relative humidity of the air of the laboratory, normal larvae hatch from these eggs (Jacobs et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jacobs et al., 2013.

claim: Tc-zen1 is only expressed in the early serosa.
source: As Tc-zen1 is only expressed in the early serosa (van der Zee et al., 2005) and is not expressed anymore by the time the experiments are performed (See discussion), we expect only to find effects that are a consequence of the absence of the serosa.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to van der Zee et al., 2005.

claim: Septic injury introduced on average 53 bacteria into wild-type eggs and 49 into serosa-less eggs.
source: Septic injury introduced on average 53 bacteria into wild-type eggs and 49 into serosa-less eggs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and described in the text.

claim: Bacterial numbers increased to 747 cfu's in wild-type eggs and to 7260 cfu's in serosa-less eggs at t=6.
source: These numbers increased on average to 747 cfu's in wild-type eggs and to 7260 cfu's in serosa-less eggs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and described in the text.

claim: The specific bacterial growth rate k in wild-type eggs is 0.44 hr−1.
source: When we use the formula N(t) = N(0)*ekt, the specific bacterial growth rate k in wild-type eggs is 0.44 hr−1, whereas k = 0.83 hr−1 in serosa-less eggs.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The specific bacterial growth rate k in serosa-less eggs is 0.83 hr−1.
source: When we use the formula N(t) = N(0)*ekt, the specific bacterial growth rate k in wild-type eggs is 0.44 hr−1, whereas k = 0.83 hr−1 in serosa-less eggs.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Illumina next generation sequencing resulted in over 970 million cDNA reads with over 49 billion bp sequence information.
source: Illumina next generation sequencing resulted in over 970 million cDNA reads with over 49 billion bp sequence information.
evidence: This is a direct report of the sequencing data obtained.

claim: Approximately 72% of the reads could be mapped to Tribolium gene models.
source: Approximately, 72% of the reads could be mapped to Tribolium gene models built on the 3.0 genome assembly (Richards et al., 2008) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct report of the mapping results from the sequencing data.

claim: Expression of 14,903 of the total of 16,541 predicted genes was found.
source: We found expression of 14,903 of the total of 16,541 predicted genes, of which 13,464 genes were expressed in wild-type, control, and Tc-zen1 RNAi eggs and 1440 genes were expressed in a subset of these treatments.
evidence: This is a direct report of the gene expression analysis results.

claim: 415 genes were differentially expressed in sterilely injured eggs compared to naive eggs.
source: This gave a total of 415 differentially expressed genes in the sterilely injured eggs compared to the naive eggs, and a total of 538 differentially regulated genes in septically injured eggs compared to naive eggs.
evidence: This is a direct report of the differential expression analysis results.

claim: 538 genes were differentially regulated in septically injured eggs compared to naive eggs.
source: This gave a total of 415 differentially expressed genes in the sterilely injured eggs compared to the naive eggs, and a total of 538 differentially regulated genes in septically injured eggs compared to naive eggs.
evidence: This is a direct report of the differential expression analysis results.

claim: Tribolium eggs possess an extensive transcriptional response upon infection.
source: This shows that Tribolium eggs possess an extensive transcriptional response upon infection.
evidence: This is inferred from the large number of differentially expressed genes upon infection.

claim: 78 immune genes were differentially regulated in wild-type eggs upon septic injury.
source: Of these genes, 78 were differentially regulated in wild-type eggs upon septic injury (Table 1 and Supplementary file 2 and 5), while 95 immune genes were differentially regulated in control RNAi eggs (Table 1 and Supplementary file 2 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Table 1 and supplementary files.

claim: 95 immune genes were differentially regulated in control RNAi eggs upon septic injury.
source: Of these genes, 78 were differentially regulated in wild-type eggs upon septic injury (Table 1 and Supplementary file 2 and 5), while 95 immune genes were differentially regulated in control RNAi eggs (Table 1 and Supplementary file 2 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Table 1 and supplementary files.

claim: RNAi itself leads to an increased number of differentially regulated genes upon bacterial challenge.
source: This indicates that RNAi itself leads to an increased number of differentially regulated genes upon bacterial challenge but, more importantly, shows that Tribolium eggs possess an elaborate immune response.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the number of differentially regulated genes in wild-type vs control RNAi eggs.

claim: PGRP-LA, LC, SA, and SB were significantly induced upon infection.
source: Of the 7 predicted peptidoglycan recognition proteins (PGRPs) in Tribolium we found significant induction of PGRP-LA, LC, SA, and SB (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAseq data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: PGRP-SA and SB were induced over 200-fold.
source: Of these PGRPs, PGRP-SA, and SB were induced over 200-fold (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAseq data shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: GNBP2 and GNBP3 were induced upon infection.
source: Of the Gram-negative binding proteins (GNBP), we found induction of GNBP2 and GNBP3 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAseq data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: 36 serine proteases and serpins were induced upon infection.
source: Interestingly, most of them seem to be functional in the immune response as we found induction of 36 serine proteases and serpins and repression of another 10 upon infection (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAseq data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: 10 serine proteases and serpins were repressed upon infection.
source: Interestingly, most of them seem to be functional in the immune response as we found induction of 36 serine proteases and serpins and repression of another 10 upon infection (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAseq data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Spz1 and spz2 were induced upon infection.
source: Of the Spaetzle ligands, we found induction of spz1 and spz2 and repression of spz4 and 5 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAseq data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Spz4 and spz5 were repressed upon infection.
source: Of the Spaetzle ligands, we found induction of spz1 and spz2 and repression of spz4 and 5 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAseq data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The toll3 receptor is significantly upregulated upon infection.
source: Interestingly, we found significant upregulation of the toll3 receptor upon infection.
evidence: This is supported by the RNAseq data.

claim: Toll3 plays a major role in the innate immune response of Tribolium.
source: This was also found in larvae and adults (Altincicek et al., 2013; Behrens et al., 2014) and suggests that it is not toll1, but toll3 that plays a major role in the innate immune response of Tribolium.
evidence: This is inferred from the upregulation data and supported by citations to similar findings in other life stages.

claim: Tribolium eggs can induce AMPs to comparable levels as larvae and adults.
source: This means that Tribolium eggs can induce AMPs to comparable levels as larvae and adults (Altincicek et al., 2013; Behrens et al., 2014).
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAseq data showing >500-fold upregulation and comparison to cited studies.

claim: Prophenoloxidase1 (proPO1) is upregulated upon infection.
source: We also found upregulation of prophenoloxidase1 (proPO1), a gene involved in melanisation, and of heme peroxidase 11, a dual oxidase (DUOX) ortholog involved in the production of reactive oxygen species (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAseq data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Heme peroxidase 11 is upregulated upon infection.
source: We also found upregulation of prophenoloxidase1 (proPO1), a gene involved in melanisation, and of heme peroxidase 11, a dual oxidase (DUOX) ortholog involved in the production of reactive oxygen species (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAseq data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: 20 potential new AMPs were identified based on antimicrobial properties.
source: Based on these criteria, we found 20 potential new AMPs (Table 2, we included the properties of several known AMPs as a reference).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the RNAseq data using specific criteria for AMP properties, shown in Table 2.

claim: 481 genes are only responsive in eggs with a serosa.
source: Of all 538 genes differentially regulated upon bacterial challenge, 481 genes are only responsive in eggs with a serosa.
evidence: This is derived from comparing the transcriptomes of wild-type, control, and Tc-zen1 RNAi eggs.

claim: 276 genes are differentially regulated in both wild-type and control eggs but not in serosa-less eggs.
source: The vast majority, 276 genes, are differentially regulated in both wild-type and control eggs but not in serosa-less eggs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in the Venn diagram in Figure 4B.

claim: Only 57 genes are differentially regulated upon microbial challenge in serosa-less Tc-zen1 RNAi eggs.
source: In the serosa-less Tc-zen1 RNAi eggs, merely 57 genes are differentially regulated upon microbial challenge, despite our finding that RNAi rather increases the number of immune responsive genes.
evidence: This is derived from the differential expression analysis of Tc-zen1 RNAi eggs.

claim: Only nine immune genes were differentially regulated upon infection in serosa-less eggs.
source: Of all 368 Tribolium genes that are annotated as immune genes (Zou et al., 2007; Altincicek et al., 2013), only nine were differentially regulated upon infection in serosa-less eggs (Table 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: None of the AMPs is induced upon infection in serosa-less eggs.
source: Notably, none of the AMPs is induced upon infection in serosa-less eggs, neither proPO1 nor the DUOX ortholog Hpx11 (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the RNAseq data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The serosa is essential for the early immune response of the Tribolium egg.
source: Thus, the serosa is essential for the early immune response of the Tribolium egg.
evidence: This is inferred from the dramatic reduction in immune gene expression in serosa-less eggs.

claim: qPCR results match the values found in the RNAseq data.
source: The fold-changes detected by qPCR after sterile and septic injury of wild-type eggs match the values found in the RNAseq data.
evidence: This is based on comparison of qPCR results shown in Figure 5 with RNAseq data.

claim: All qPCRs showed the absence of induction in Tc-zen1 RNAi eggs.
source: Most importantly, all qPCRs convincingly showed the absence of induction in Tc-zen1 RNAi eggs, thus providing independent support for our conclusion that the serosa is required for the immune response in Tribolium eggs.
evidence: This is supported by the qPCR data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Thaumatin1 expression associates with the large polyploid serosal nuclei and not with the dense cells of the germ-band.
source: The thaumatin1 expression clearly associates with the large polyploid serosal nuclei and not with the dense cells of the germ-band (overlay in Figure 6C and C′).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 6.

claim: Thaumatin1 is expressed exclusively in the overlying serosa on the outer surface and not in the underlying embryo proper.
source: A deeper focal plane of a different egg demonstrates exclusive expression in the overlying serosa on the outer surface (Figure 6D,D′) and not in the underlying embryo proper (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 6.

claim: Attacin1 expression consistently associated with the large polyploid serosal nuclei.
source: Also attacin1 expression consistently associated with the large polyploid serosal nuclei (Figure 6G–I′).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 6.

claim: It is the serosal epithelium itself that expresses AMPs upon infection.
source: Thus, it is the serosal epithelium itself that expresses these AMPs upon infection.
evidence: This is concluded from the in situ hybridization data showing AMP expression in serosal cells.

claim: 44 immune genes have serosa-dependent expression.
source: We found 44 immune genes that have serosa-dependent expression (Table 3).
evidence: This is based on comparing transcriptomes of naive Tc-zen1 RNAi eggs to naive wild-type eggs, shown in Table 3.

claim: More than 75% of serosa-dependent immune genes are involved in the recognition of microbes and extracellular signal transduction.
source: Of these genes, more than 75% is involved in the recognition of microbes and extracellular signal transduction such as PGRP-LA, many serine proteases and Spz4 and Spz5 (Table 3).
evidence: This is calculated from the data in Table 3.

claim: The transmembrane receptor toll3 exhibits higher expression in unchallenged eggs with a serosa than in eggs without a serosa.
source: Notably, the transmembrane receptor toll3 exhibits higher expression in unchallenged eggs with a serosa than in eggs without a serosa.
evidence: This is based on comparing expression levels in naive wild-type vs Tc-zen1 RNAi eggs.

claim: The serosa is an immune competent epithelium that expresses many genes involved in bacterial recognition and transduction of this recognition to receptor activation.
source: These data indicate that the serosa is an immune competent epithelium that expresses many genes involved in bacterial recognition and transduction of this recognition to receptor activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the constitutive expression of immune genes in the serosa.

claim: Toll3 is expressed in the serosal epithelium.
source: Although toll3 was clearly expressed in the serosa (partly detached from the egg Figure 7A′), we also detected expression in the embryo.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 7.

claim: Scavenger receptor B5 shows clear expression in the serosal epithelium.
source: For scavenger receptor B5 that has a 30-fold higher expression in eggs with a serosa, we did find clear expression in the serosal epithelium (Figure 7D), whereas the underlying germ-band was not stained (Figure 7F and F′).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization shown in Figure 7.

claim: All genes listed in Table 3 are constitutively expressed in the serosa.
source: We propose that all genes listed in Table 3 are constitutively expressed in the serosa and thus make the serosa an immune-competent frontier epithelium.
evidence: This is proposed based on the differential expression data and in situ hybridization results.

claim: The number of immune-responsive genes found in the Tribolium egg is comparable to the number found in larvae.
source: The number of immune-responsive genes found in the Tribolium egg is comparable to the number found in larvae (Behrens et al., 2014) and higher than what was found in adults (Altincicek et al., 2013), but this might be due to differences in sequence coverage.
evidence: This is based on comparison to cited studies, with a caveat about technical differences.

claim: The number of immune-responsive genes found in the Tribolium egg is higher than what was found in adults.
source: The number of immune-responsive genes found in the Tribolium egg is comparable to the number found in larvae (Behrens et al., 2014) and higher than what was found in adults (Altincicek et al., 2013), but this might be due to differences in sequence coverage.
evidence: This is based on comparison to cited studies, with a caveat about technical differences.

claim: Both the Toll and IMD pathways are utilized in the immune response of the Tribolium egg.
source: The induction of several genes from both the Toll and IMD pathway indicates that both pathways are utilized in the immune response of the Tribolium egg.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNAseq data showing induction of genes from both pathways.

claim: Toll signaling is involved in innate immunity in the egg.
source: It is striking that Toll signaling seems to be involved in innate immunity in the egg, because Toll signaling at this stage has only been associated with developmental functions until now (Leulier and Lemaitre, 2008; Nunes da Fonseca et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and contrasted with previous knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Tc-zen1 is practically not expressed at the time experiments were performed.
source: Indeed, we found only three RNAseq reads that map to Tc-zen1, confirming that Tc-zen1 is practically not expressed at the time we performed experiments.
evidence: This is based on the RNAseq data showing minimal Tc-zen1 expression.

claim: The lack of the full-range immune response after Tc-zen1 RNAi is exclusively due to the absence of the serosa.
source: Thus, we are confident to conclude that the lack of the full-range immune response after Tc-zen1 RNAi is exclusively due to the absence of the serosa.
evidence: This is concluded based on the timing of Tc-zen1 expression and the RNAi effects.

claim: The serosa is a frontier epithelium that provides the insect egg with a full-range immune response.
source: We conclude that the serosa is a frontier epithelium that provides the insect egg with a full-range immune response.
evidence: This is the main conclusion based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: The separation of the serosal cells from the germ rudiment is the first morphological distinction that can be made in the blastoderm of the developing egg.
source: Interestingly, the separation of the serosal cells from the germ rudiment is the first morphological distinction that can be made in the blastoderm of the developing egg (Handel et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Handel et al., 2000.

claim: The serosal cells envelop the complete embryo before the ectoderm starts to differentiate.
source: The serosal cells will have enveloped the complete embryo before the ectoderm starts to differentiate.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about serosa development.

claim: The polyploid nuclei allow the serosal cells to quickly synthesize large amounts of proteins.
source: In addition, the polyploid nuclei allow the serosal cells to quickly synthesize large amounts of proteins providing protection for the vulnerable developing embryo.
evidence: This is inferred from the known properties of polyploid cells.

claim: The serosa was lost in the Schizophoran flies.
source: Drosophila eggs do not develop a serosa, as this extraembryonic membrane was lost in the Schizophoran flies (Schmidt-Ott, 2000; Rafiqi et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schmidt-Ott, 2000 and Rafiqi et al., 2008.

claim: A trade-off with developmental speed might have driven the loss of the serosa in Schizophoran flies.
source: A trade-off with developmental speed might have driven the loss of the serosa in these flies living on ephemeral food sources (Jacobs et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation.

claim: The absence of the serosa in the Schizophora accounts for the poor immune response of Drosophila eggs.
source: We suggest that the absence of the serosa in the Schizophora accounts for the poor immune response of Drosophila eggs.
evidence: This is suggested based on the findings in Tribolium and comparison to Drosophila.

claim: All other insects possess a serosa.
source: Since all other insects possess a serosa, we propose that early immune competence is a general property of insect eggs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about insect anatomy.

claim: Early immune competence is a general property of insect eggs.
source: Since all other insects possess a serosa, we propose that early immune competence is a general property of insect eggs.
evidence: This is proposed based on the findings in Tribolium and the widespread presence of the serosa in insects.

claim: Tribolium castaneum eggs can mount a full-range innate immune response involving antimicrobial peptides, melanisation, and the production of reactive oxygen species.
source: Tribolium castaneum eggs can mount a full-range innate immune response involving antimicrobial peptides, melanisation, and the production of reactive oxygen species.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the Conclusions section, based on all experimental data.

claim: The immune response in Tribolium eggs depends entirely on the extraembryonic serosa.
source: This response depends entirely on the extraembryonic serosa, an immune competent frontier epithelium that is absent in Drosophila.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the Conclusions section, based on all experimental data.
